plan.summary: The two genuinely on-target pet publishers are direct competitors, so the plan is deliberately thin: no core-budget recommendation, and two tests — Tailcrate for confirmed dog owners already buying subscriptions, Pantrygood for clean-ingredient premium subscribers — while the wellness and apparel placements scored on income and price alone are excluded for having no link to a senior dog.

test.name: Tailcrate
test.adjacent_conflict: sells pet_subscription_box, pet_treats, a close substitute
test.rationale: Every checkout here is a confirmed dog owner already buying on subscription, so a food subscription is a natural next line item; the open question is dog age, since the audience is "Millennials treating dogs as family" at 25-45 and likely owns younger dogs than a senior formula serves.
test.risk: Tone and price mismatch: "Fun, playful brand voice converts best" against clinical vet-formulated messaging, and a $75 subscription start is 2x the $35 typical basket; the senior-dog share of this young audience may be small.

test.name: Pantrygood
test.rationale: These are values-driven, high-income subscription grocery buyers "Responsive to clean-ingredient, sustainability, and wellness claims" — the same grain-free, vet-formulated argument the brand makes — and an $86 typical basket means a $75 first order is in range; worth measuring because dog ownership is unknown here.

evidence.quote: Responsive to clean-ingredient, sustainability, and wellness claims

test.risk: No pet signal at all in the record, so the addressable share of this traffic (senior-dog households) could be small enough to sink CPA.

bid_strategy.rationale: $75 first order (assumed) × 0.60 = $45.00 target CPA: subscription revenue repeats, so a first order can be bought at a larger share of its value. The max CPA allows headroom while the campaign learns over 14 days.

test_plan.promote_if: CPA at or below the $45.00 target after 14 days: move it to core.
test_plan.cut_if: CPA above the $58.50 maximum, or no conversions after 14 days: stop it.

test_plan.hypothesis: These are values-driven, high-income subscription grocery buyers "Responsive to clean-ingredient, sustainability, and wellness claims" — the same grain-free, vet-formulated argument the brand makes — and an $86 typical basket means a $75 first order is in range; worth measuring because dog ownership is unknown here.
test_plan.risk: No pet signal at all in the record, so the addressable share of this traffic (senior-dog households) could be small enough to sink CPA.
test_plan.promote_if: CPA at or below the $45.00 target after 14 days: move it to core.
test_plan.cut_if: CPA above the $58.50 maximum, or no conversions after 14 days: stop it.

frequency_cap.rationale: Offers appear once, right after checkout; repeating them reads as spam.

experiment.graduate_rule: After 14 days, move a test publisher to core if its CPA is at or below target; cut any placement above max CPA.

launch_summary.summary: The full $10,000 runs as a test, split evenly between Tailcrate and Pantrygood, because no publisher scored well enough to be a core buy and the two best-matched pet sites are direct competitors. Tailcrate tests whether confirmed dog-owning subscribers include enough senior-dog households; Pantrygood tests whether clean-ingredient, high-income grocery subscribers own dogs at all. Both graduate to core at or below the $45.00 target cost per new customer after 14 days and get cut above $58.50.
uncertainties: The $75 first order is assumed, and both the $45.00 target and $58.50 maximum cost per new customer are built on it.

Neither publisher confirms senior-dog ownership — Tailcrate skews to a younger 25-45 audience, and Pantrygood has no pet signal at all — so the reachable share of traffic could be too small to hit target.
Tailcrate's playful brand voice and $35 typical basket sit against clinical vet-formulated messaging and a $75 subscription start.
